Introduction

Vienna, the capital of Austria, is famous for its world-famous coffee houses and its legendary Wiener schnitzel. The Guardian piece says there is more to the Austrian capital's cuisine than schnitzel, with dishes from all over the world. The piece argues that Vienna's cuisine reflects Europe's history of empire and cultural exchange, with dishes drawn from all corners of the globe. It presents a city where food is more than a sign of joie de vivre — the Viennese love to eat, and sometimes it is just hunger.

Vienna's dishes come from all over the world: Galicians, the French, Italians, Bohemians, Hungarians and Poles all played a part. The city has a long history of decline, and entire empires have crumbled here — yet Vienna's cuisine has outlasted them all. Emperors took a final sigh and slipped under the table, ministers burst while tucking into their dessert, and Vienna's cuisine outlasted them all.

The piece traces Vienna's cuisine to dishes drawn from all corners of the globe, the legacy of an empire that no longer exists. Its central line is that the spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna.

Sources

  • The Guardian – "The spirit of a borderless Europe steams from the pots and pans of Vienna" (2026-11-21)

Conclusion

Vienna's cuisine has outlasted empires, and the Viennese take food seriously — without coming across as particularly serious. The piece links the city's food to its history, and the legacy is an empire that no longer exists, with dishes drawn from all corners of the globe. Outside the coffee house, the world passes by; inside, the coffee goes cold — and in a world where free time is organised down to the last minute, that is a considerable luxury.

The steam rising from Vienna's pots and pans carries the spirit of a borderless Europe.

Key takeaways

  • Vienna's cuisine is more than schnitzel: its dishes come from all over the world.
  • The city's food is a record of its history: the legacy of an empire that no longer exists.
  • The Viennese take food seriously, but without coming across as particularly serious.
  • Vienna's pots and pans steam with the spirit of a borderless Europe.
  • A schnitzel is fried gently, a strudel is rolled out with patience and care, and a goulash is left to simmer until the onions have almost dissolved.
